passage:
Dear Anjali,
I'm writing this on paper because I know you read messages ten times looking for hidden meaning, and I wanted you to have something you can hold. You cancelled the planetarium again on Saturday, twenty minutes before. I won't pretend I wasn't disappointed. But I'm not angry, and I don't think you're being dramatic. I've seen your hands shake before you walk into a crowded place. So here's my plan: I'll keep inviting you. Every time. If you can come, great. If you can't, I'll send you a photo of whatever we saw. And no one-letter replies from me, I promise; I'll write full sentences.
Your friend,
Varun

qa.q: How long before the planetarium trip did Anjali cancel?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What does Varun believe about why Anjali cancels?
qa.a: Varun doesn't think Anjali is being dramatic, having seen Anjali's hands shake before crowded places.

qa.q: What choice does Varun make about future plans?
qa.a: Varun decides to keep inviting Anjali every time and to send photos when Anjali can't come, staying steady and consistent.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel on reading that the invitations will keep coming?
qa.a: Anjali may feel less alone and less guilty, knowing that cancelling won't end the friendship.

grounding: A friend writes to Anjali, who overthinks messages and cancels at the last minute, promising patient, steady invitations.

passage: You asked why I keep my phone on loud at night, Didi. It's Pema. If I reply "ok" instead of "okay!!", she spends an hour wondering if I'm angry with her. She's told me so: "Disha, I thought you were angry." She cancels outings at the last minute, and at first I thought she was just flaking. Then one day at the bus stop I saw her face go white when a big group got on, and she stepped back and let the bus go. That's not drama. So I changed a few things. I send voice notes, so she can hear I'm fine. I tell her plans early, with who's coming. And when she cancels, I just say, "No worries, next time," and I mean it. Last week she came to the whole birthday party.

qa.q: What did Pema do at the bus stop when a big group got on?
qa.a: Her face went white, and she stepped back and let the bus go.

qa.q: What worries Pema when a reply is short?
qa.a: She worries Disha is angry with her and spends an hour wondering about it.

qa.q: What changes did Disha make after the bus stop moment?
qa.a: Disha sent voice notes, shared plans early with who was coming, and answered cancellations with a calm "next time".

qa.q: How might Pema have felt going to the whole birthday party?
qa.a: She may have felt safer because Disha had been steady and patient, so the party felt less frightening.

grounding: A teenager describes Pema, who overthinks messages and cancels plans, and how patience and consistency help her feel less alone.

passage: I'm Madhav, and I've sat next to Aditi since Class 8. Here's what I've seen. She'll type a message to the group, delete it, type it again, and ask me, 'Does this sound rude?' It never does. Last Saturday we'd planned the science museum. At 9.40, twenty minutes before, she texted: 'So sorry, can't come, not feeling great.' Some of the group rolled their eyes. 'Drama again,' Rohit said. I felt a flash of annoyance too, honestly. But I've seen her hands shake before she goes somewhere new. I don't know what goes on in her head. So I texted back: 'No problem. Want me to send you pictures? Same plan next Saturday?' She sent a thumbs-up. On Monday she gave me a small drawing of the dinosaur skeleton from my photos. The next Saturday, she came.

qa.q: What time did Aditi text to cancel?
qa.a: At 9.40, twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What did Madhav feel when Aditi cancelled?
qa.a: Madhav felt a flash of annoyance at first, then chose patience, having seen Aditi's hands shake before new places.

qa.q: Why was Madhav's reply a good one?
qa.a: It was calm and steady, offering photos and the same plan next week, so Aditi felt included rather than judged.

qa.q: What might Aditi feel when friends call it 'drama'?
qa.a: She would likely feel ashamed and more alone, when she is anxious rather than seeking attention.

grounding: Shows a classmate who sees an anxious friend overthink messages and cancel at the last minute, and responds with patient, steady consistency.

passage:
Monday. Rashmi held out the phone for the fifth time. 'Read it again. Does "Could you check my marks?" sound rude to Ma'am?' Gargi sighed. 'Just send it!' Rashmi went quiet and didn't send it at all. Gargi felt bad the whole bus ride home.
Thursday. Twenty minutes before the movie, Rashmi texted: 'Sorry, can't. Stomach.' Gargi's thumb hovered over 'again??'. She deleted it. 'Okay. Next time I'm saving you the good seat.'
Sunday. Gargi turned up at Rashmi's door with popcorn and a film on her laptop. 'Couch cinema. No crowd.' Halfway through, Rashmi said quietly, 'Thanks for not giving up on me.' Gargi passed the popcorn. 'Same time next week?'

qa.q: What did Rashmi text before the movie?
qa.a: 'Sorry, can't. Stomach.'

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after telling Rashmi to 'just send it'?
qa.a: Gargi felt bad and a little guilty the whole bus ride, having seen Rashmi go quiet.

qa.q: What did Gargi change between Monday and Sunday?
qa.a: Gargi swapped impatience for steady patience: deleting 'again??', keeping plans open, and bringing a quiet movie night to Rashmi's home.

qa.q: What does Rashmi's 'Thanks for not giving up on me' suggest?
qa.a: Rashmi had probably feared that friends would lose patience, and felt relieved and less alone with Gargi's steadiness.

grounding: Shows a classmate who learns to meet an anxious friend's overthinking and last-minute cancelling with patience and consistency.

passage: Jeevan, you say your friend keeps backing out of plans and you're fed up. Let me tell you about my friend Nikhil. When your Anand Mama was fifteen, in Nagpur, Nikhil was the cleverest boy in our class, and the most nervous. He'd write a note to a teacher and tear it up four times. Every Sunday he'd promise to come for cricket, and every Sunday, at the last minute, his little brother would come running: 'Nikhil's not coming.' The other boys said he was just making a fuss. I was fed up too. Then one Sunday, instead of shouting over his wall, I walked in and sat on his steps. He looked so ashamed. 'I get scared before things. I don't know why.' So I stopped asking him to the big match. I asked him to bowl to me, just the two of us, in the lane. He came every week after that.

qa.q: How many times would Nikhil tear up a note?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Anand feel about Nikhil's cancelling at first?
qa.a: Anand felt fed up and frustrated, just like the other boys.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the friendship?
qa.a: Anand walked in and sat on Nikhil's steps instead of shouting, heard that Nikhil got scared before things, and switched to a small two-person game.

qa.q: What was it like for Nikhil when the boys said he was just making a fuss?
qa.a: Nikhil felt ashamed and more alone, since he was genuinely scared before things and didn't know why.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager who stops seeing an anxious friend's cancelling as fuss and offers steady, patient company instead.

passage:
The film started at six, and it was already 5:40 when Jyoti's phone buzzed under the bus shelter. Rain was hammering the roof.
Jasleen: sorry sorry I can't come. I think I read Mehak's message wrong and now it'll be awkward
Jyoti sighed. It was the third time this month. Her first thought was to type "you always do this". She deleted it.
Instead she wrote: "Okay. The film's on again Sunday afternoon. I'll save you a seat either way."
She added: "Want me to look at Mehak's message with you after?"
The bus came, and Jyoti watched the film alone, a little disappointed. Afterwards she called. Jasleen read the message aloud; it was only "k". "She sends 'k' to everyone," Jyoti said. Jasleen laughed shakily.
On Sunday, Jasleen came. She held Jyoti's sleeve at the door, but she came.

qa.q: What time did the film start?
qa.a: The film started at six.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when Jasleen cancelled, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little disappointed, since it was the third time that month, but she deleted "you always do this" and wrote a calm reply instead.

qa.q: Which of Jyoti's choices helped Jasleen most?
qa.a: Offering the Sunday show and a saved seat "either way", then calling to look at Mehak's message together, showed steady support without blame.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jasleen to cancel again?
qa.a: Jasleen seems embarrassed and caught in overthinking the message; hearing a patient reply instead of anger probably made it easier for her to come on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a teen staying patient and consistent with a friend who overthinks messages and cancels plans, which helps the friend feel less alone.
